The Book of the Dead. An ancient Egyptian funerary text that guided souls through the afterlife, used from around 1550 BC to about 50 BC. It was a collection of magical spells, incantations, and formulas placed in tombs to help the deceased navigate the dangers of the underworld, known as Duat, and achieve a blessed afterlife.

The original Egyptian title translates to the Book of the Coming Forth by Day, or the Book of Spells for Coming Forth by Day. These texts were typically written in hieroglyphic or hieratic script on papyrus scrolls, often decorated with elaborate illustrations called vignettes that depicted the journey of the soul.

At the heart of the Book of the Dead lay instructions for the Weighing of the Heart ceremony. The jackal-headed god Anubis would weigh the deceased's heart against the feather of Ma'at, the principle of truth and justice. Before 42 judges of the underworld, the dead were required to recite the Negative Confession, also called the Declaration of Innocence, denying they had committed any of 42 specific sins.

The text is traditionally attributed to Thoth, the ibis-headed god of writing and scribes, who served as its author and divine custodian. One of the most famous surviving copies is the Papyrus of Ani, a lavishly illustrated version created around 1250 BC for a royal scribe named Ani. The Book of the Dead provided everything needed for the soul's journey, from practical spells to moral declarations that would determine whether the deceased could pass beyond the underworld and enter eternal peace.
